mcqs.question: A VPN gives a connecting device two things. Besides encrypting the traffic, what's the other mechanism, and why does it matter?
options: Network membership — the device is treated as if it were physically on the private network, usually without further per-request checks
Automatic malware scanning of the device before it connects
A guarantee that the connecting user's password hasn't been compromised
Load balancing of internal traffic across data centers
mcqs.explanation: The membership grant is the half of a VPN with the bigger security consequence: once connected, the device is generally trusted at the network level for the rest of the session. Malware scanning, password-compromise guarantees, and load balancing are not things a VPN tunnel itself provides.

mcqs.question: Why do SSL/TLS VPNs more naturally support scoping access to specific applications than IPSec VPNs do?
options: SSL/TLS VPNs don't support remote workers, only site-to-site links
IPSec VPNs cannot use encryption stronger than 128-bit keys
SSL/TLS VPNs operate higher in the stack, over TLS, which makes it natural to present and gate access per application rather than per whole subnet
SSL/TLS VPNs require a dedicated hardware client on every device
mcqs.explanation: Operating at the transport/application layer over TLS makes it straightforward to build an access portal that gates individual applications, rather than tunneling arbitrary IP traffic the way IPSec does by default. IPSec is the one more associated with site-to-site links and heavier clients, not SSL/TLS, and the encryption-strength claim is unrelated to this distinction.

mcqs.question: What is the core trust problem with a traditional VPN, once a session is established?
options: It re-authenticates the user every few minutes, which slows workflows
It encrypts traffic too slowly for real-time applications
It cannot be used from mobile devices
It authenticates once at connection time and then generally trusts the traffic as network traffic, without re-checking identity or device posture during the session
mcqs.explanation: The one-time check at connection time, followed by broad, un-re-verified trust for the rest of the session, is exactly the gap zero trust is designed to close. VPNs don't force frequent re-authentication (if anything, too little), and neither encryption speed, mobile support, nor IP version is the core issue here.

mcqs.question: Why have VPN concentrators (gateways) become an especially attractive target for attackers, beyond just being internet-facing?
options: They are the only internet-facing systems most companies run
A single vulnerability in the appliance can grant a path around authentication entirely or expose many users' sessions, concentrating value that a single stolen credential doesn't have
They never receive security patches from vendors
They are exempt from most companies' vulnerability scanning programs by policy
mcqs.explanation: Because the gateway sits between the internet and internal network access for every remote user, breaking the appliance itself can be worth more than any one credential — several major real intrusions started exactly this way. Vendors do patch these appliances (the risk is patching lag, not absence of patches), they aren't the only internet-facing system, and no policy exempts them from scanning — that's the operational failure the slide warns about.

mcqs.question: A team builds an internal admin API with weak authentication, reasoning "it's only reachable over the VPN, so it's safe." What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: VPN traffic cannot reach internal APIs at all, so the API would be unreachable
It makes the VPN gateway's one-time connection check the only thing standing between the internet and that API, once any credential or session is compromised
APIs cannot be exposed over a VPN tunnel by design
The VPN would automatically add strong authentication to any service behind it
mcqs.explanation: "On the VPN" only tells you a tunnel was authenticated at connection time — it says nothing about the current state of that device or session, so treating it as a substitute for the API's own authentication collapses the whole defense to one check. VPNs don't block API traffic, don't refuse to carry it, and don't add authentication to anything behind them automatically.
